title: The Haskalah
hook: the Jewish Enlightenment, joining Jewish and general learning

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses Mendelssohn: the Torah in German, printed in Hebrew letters. Your line was two worlds. What did you carry from one into the other? Today, the movement that grew up around people like him. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

How do you say telescope in the language of the Psalms? Or vaccine, or electricity, or newspaper? The Bible never needed those words. Hebrew had long been a language of prayer, study and law, while people spoke something else at home. Then a group of Jewish writers decided Hebrew should be able to talk about everything: planets and poetry, chemistry and history. They printed journals in Hebrew about science. They wrote Hebrew poems that had nothing to do with the synagogue. They were stretching an ancient language to fit a new world. Today, the movement they belonged to.
screen: `TELESCOPE, IN THE LANGUAGE OF THE PSALMS?` → `HEBREW FOR EVERYTHING.` → `AN ANCIENT LANGUAGE, A NEW WORLD.`

segments.voice: The movement is called the Haskalah, the Jewish Enlightenment, and its followers were called maskilim. It began among Jews in Germany in Mendelssohn's circle, and later moved east, into the towns and cities of the Pale. The maskilim had a program. Jews, they said, should learn the languages of the countries they lived in, and mathematics, science, history and useful trades, alongside the Torah, not instead of it. They wanted Jewish schools that taught both. And they wanted Hebrew itself reborn as a living language of literature. They liked to point back to scholars like Maimonides, who had studied philosophy and medicine and wrote some of the great works of Jewish law. There's an old line in the Mishnah that fits their hopes. In Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma asks: who is wise? And he answers: the one who learns from every person. Wisdom, on that reading, can come from anywhere, and a learned Jew can take it in without losing who they are. That was the maskilim's bet. Not everyone accepted it, and the argument was fierce. Traditional rabbis, Hasidic and non-Hasidic alike, warned that the Haskalah was a road out of Judaism, and they could point to young people who walked it all the way out. Some maskilim, in turn, mocked the traditional world, sometimes cruelly. Each camp had its own picture of what Jewish life should look like in a new age. And meanwhile the Hebrew journals kept printing, stretching the language of the Psalms to name things it had never named before.
screen: `THE MASKILIM AND THEIR PROGRAM.` · `TORAH AND THE WORLD'S LEARNING.` · `WHO IS WISE? WHO LEARNS FROM EVERYONE.` · then, large: `A FIERCE ARGUMENT, AND HEBREW STRETCHING.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one secular thing with Jewish eyes. Breathe in slowly, and out. Bring to mind something from the ordinary world that you know a little about: how plants grow, how money works, a piece of music, a law of physics. Hold it up and turn it slowly, the way a maskil might. Ask: what in this would a Torah teacher find worth noticing? A pattern, a kind of order, a question about how to live? You don't need an answer. Just look at one ordinary thing from two angles at once. The bell holds the time.
Haskalah. The Jewish Enlightenment: joining Torah with general learning, and reviving Hebrew as a language for everything. Its followers were the maskilim. Today's word.
Your line: enlightenment. Today, learn one new fact about the world, and ask what Ben Zoma might say: who did I learn it from? Day nine hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: The Haskalah's legacy lives on in modern Hebrew literature and in Jewish schools that teach both Jewish and general subjects, while some traditional communities still keep secular learning at a distance.
